subject: errors using new lme4 and lmerTest updates

messages.subject: errors using new lme4 and lmerTest updates
parts:
Hi folks --

I'm in Plant Pathology working on forest ecology and disease questions.  I've been on your e-mail list but haven't made it to a meeting because I'm only on campus a couple days a week.  I'm wondering if someone might be able to chat about an analysis stumbling block I've hit with the recent updates to the lme4 package.

I am running a lot of generalized linear mixed effects models in lme4.  The data are hierarchical in that some measures are taken on tree stems that occur in multi-stemmed trees that occur within the same forest plot.  There is therefore a random effect of tree nested within plot (1|Plot/TreeID) and of tree species (1|Species) as there may be variation in the responses among species. Some of the models have Gaussian errors and some are logistic-type regressions with binomial errors, all with the same random effects as above.  I've used lme4 quite extensively in the past.

My models were mostly running just fine last summer, but I've been getting new errors with the re-vamp of lme4 that occurred last August.  I'm trying to narrow down whether these are bugs in the package, quirks of my data that weren't previously triggering errors, or some sort of fundamental flaw that's going to necessitate a whole new approach.  I tend to get different errors as I update packages to ever more recent releases.  First it was along the lines of "Downdated VtV is not positive definite;" now it has changed to errors in the optimizer, failure to converge, and problems with the Hessian matrix.  I need a better understanding of the matrix algebra underlying the models to figure out what's going on.

To add further complication, the models are also part of a path analysis using hierarchical models following the methods of Shipley's 2009 Ecology paper.  Without getting into too many details of the path analysis method, the errors tend to occur with paths at a particular level of the data hierarchy, while other models are just fine.

Is any of this in the realm of familiarity for anyone?  Can I buy you coffee and brainstorm with you?

Thanks,
Margaret
